A Quick Guide to Go's Assembler

entries.description: you plan to write assembly language
entries.subject: you plan

spans.text: If you plan to write assembly language, you should read that document although much of it is Plan 9-specific.

If you want to see what the instructions look like in assembly for a given architecture, say amd64, there are many examples in the sources of the standard library, in packages such as runtime and math/big.

entries.description: assembly code to interact with Go
entries.subject: assembly code

spans.text: The current document provides a summary of the syntax and the differences with what is explained in that document, and describes the peculiarities that apply when writing assembly code to interact with Go.

entries.description: important thing to know about Go's assembler is that it is not a direct representation of the underlying machine
entries.subject: important thing
entries.object: know about Go's assembler is that it is not a direct representation of the underlying machine

spans.text: The most important thing to know about Go's assembler is that it is not a direct representation of the underlying machine.
Some of the details map precisely to the machine, but some do not.

entries.task_id: correspond exactly|to|the machine instruction with that name
entries.description: correspond exactly to the machine instruction with that name
entries.subject: correspond exactly
entries.object: the machine instruction with that name

spans.text: Or it might correspond exactly to the machine instruction with that name.

entries.description: operations tend to appear as themselves
entries.subject: operations tend

spans.text: In general, machine-specific operations tend to appear as themselves, while more general concepts like memory move and subroutine call and return are more abstract.
The assembler program is a way to parse a description of that semi-abstract instruction set and turn it into instructions to be input to the linker.

The distinction rarely matters but to avoid ambiguity, division or right shift where the right operand's high bit is set is rejected.
Some symbols, such as R1 or LR, are predefined and refer to registers.
There are four predeclared symbols that refer to pseudo-registers.
The compilers maintain a virtual frame pointer and refer to the arguments on the stack as offsets from that pseudo-register.
• SB: Static base pointer: global symbols.

entries.task_id: is used|to|name global functions and data
entries.description: is used to name global functions and data
entries.subject: is used

spans.text: This form is used to name global functions and data.
The FP pseudo-register is a virtual frame pointer used to refer to function arguments.

entries.task_id: an offset|to|the name refers to that offset from the symbol's address
entries.description: an offset to the name refers to that offset from the symbol's address
entries.subject: an offset
entries.object: the name refers to that offset from the symbol's address

spans.text: Adding an offset to the name refers to that offset from the symbol's address, so foo+4(SB) is four bytes past the start of foo.
Thus 0(FP) is the first argument to the function, 8(FP) is the second (on a 64-bit machine), and so on.

entries.task_id: when referring|to|a function argument this way
entries.description: when referring to a function argument this way
entries.subject: when referring

spans.text: However, when referring to a function argument this way, it is necessary to place a name at the beginning, as in first_arg+0(FP) and second_arg+8(FP).

folded.id: an offset|to|the name refers to that offset from the symbol's address
folded.subject: an offset
folded.object: the name refers to that offset from the symbol's address

spans.text: Adding an offset to the name refers to that offset from the symbol's address, so foo+4(SB) is four bytes past the start of foo.
Some symbols, such as R1 or LR, are predefined and refer to registers.
There are four predeclared symbols that refer to pseudo-registers.
The compilers maintain a virtual frame pointer and refer to the arguments on the stack as offsets from that pseudo-register.

The current document provides a summary of the syntax and the differences with what is explained in that document, and describes the peculiarities that apply when writing assembly code to interact with Go.
The assembler program is a way to parse a description of that semi-abstract instruction set and turn it into instructions to be input to the linker.

Thus 0(FP) is the first argument to the function, 8(FP) is the second (on a 64-bit machine), and so on.

spans.text: The most important thing to know about Go's assembler is that it is not a direct representation of the underlying machine.

folded.id: is used|to|name global functions and data
folded.subject: is used

spans.text: This form is used to name global functions and data.
The FP pseudo-register is a virtual frame pointer used to refer to function arguments.
Some of the details map precisely to the machine, but some do not.
The distinction rarely matters but to avoid ambiguity, division or right shift where the right operand's high bit is set is rejected.

folded.id: when referring|to|a function argument this way
folded.subject: when referring

spans.text: However, when referring to a function argument this way, it is necessary to place a name at the beginning, as in first_arg+0(FP) and second_arg+8(FP).
If you plan to write assembly language, you should read that document although much of it is Plan 9-specific.

If you want to see what the instructions look like in assembly for a given architecture, say amd64, there are many examples in the sources of the standard library, in packages such as runtime and math/big.
